summary:
kisht. (Tajik for "sowing") is a free web tool that tells a farmer what to plant on their own field for the next four years, season by season, and explains why. It is built first for farmers in Tajikistan, where agriculture employs about 43% of workers but only 5% of the land is arable.

The farmer drops a pin on a 3D globe and sets the field size in sotka or hectares. kisht. pulls NASA Earth observations for that exact spot: 30 years of climate and root-zone soil moisture from NASA POWER, the groundwater trend from GRACE / GRACE-FO and slope from SRTM, plus soil carbon and pH from SoilGrids. It shows in plain words what has changed since the 1990s, then builds rotations that fit the field and the farmer's priority: save water, build soil, income or reliability. Every plan can be stress-tested against +2 °C and −20 % rain, and "Why this plan" links each crop to the data behind it.

Example: for a cotton–wheat field in the Vakhsh valley (Khatlon), with about 310 mm of rain a year and 38 °C summers, kisht. suggests pearl millet, sorghum, chickpea, sesame and potato alongside wheat. Soil goes from fair to good and the fit for the field rises from 62% to 76%. As a check, our GRACE trend for Punjab, India (−4.2 cm a year) matches published research (Rodell et al., 2009, Nature).

details:
WHAT IT DOES

kisht. (Tajik for "sowing") answers the question every farmer asks before a season: what should I plant on my field next, and why? It turns NASA Earth observations into a concrete four-year crop rotation, season by season, for any field on Earth. It is built first for Tajikistan, where agriculture employs about 43% of workers but only 5% of the land is arable, so every field counts.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Your field.

The farmer drops a pin on a 3D globe and sets the field size in sotka, hectares or km². kisht. loads data for that exact spot: soil texture, organic carbon and pH (SoilGrids, 250 m) and elevation and slope (NASA SRTM).

2. What changed.

kisht. compares 1996–2005 with 2016–2025 using NASA POWER (temperature, rainfall, root-zone soil moisture) and the GRACE / GRACE-FO groundwater trend, and explains the change in plain words.

3. What to sow.

A rule-based engine builds 4-year rotations (2 seasons per year) from a crop table based on FAO Irrigation & Drainage Papers 56, 33 and 29. Agronomic rules: no same crop family twice in a row, a cereal every year, a legume when soil carbon is low, soil-holding crops on steep slopes, and a penalty for thirsty crops when groundwater is falling. The farmer picks what matters most: balanced, save water, build soil, income or reliability. Every plan is compared with the farmer's current rotation and can be stress-tested against +2 °C and −20 % rain. "Why this plan" links every decision to the exact number and dataset behind it.

EXAMPLE: VAKHSH VALLEY, KHATLON

NASA POWER shows about 310 mm of rain a year and summer highs of 38 °C; GRACE shows water storage roughly stable (−0.7 cm/yr); SRTM shows a flat 1.5% slope; SoilGrids gives organic carbon 1.2% and pH 7.9. Today's rotation, cotton then wheat every year, scores only "fair" on soil and fits the field at 62%. The best plan from kisht.: pearl millet and chickpea (2027–2028), sorghum and potato (2029), sesame and wheat (2030). Drought- and heat-tolerant millet and sorghum suit the dry, hot summers; chickpea puts nitrogen back into the soil; four crop families instead of two break pest cycles. Soil rises to "good", reliability to "strong", and fit to 76%. The honest trade-off: income drops from "strong" to "good", so a farmer focused on money can choose the "Highest income" plan instead.

VALIDATION

Our GRACE trend for Punjab, India (−4.2 cm/yr) matches published research (Rodell et al., 2009, Nature). A Python script re-checks our cached demo data against the live NASA POWER API (0 differences). 151 automated tests cover the engine and data handling.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- Healthier soil through legumes and crop-family diversity.

- Crops that fit the real rain and heat of the field.

- Plans that hold up in a hotter, drier future.

- Free, no sign-up, runs in the browser and on a phone, in Tajik, Russian and English — for dehkan farms and smallholders, and for agronomists as a data-backed starting point.

Next step: a pilot with farmers and agronomists in Khatlon and Sughd. kisht. supports farmers; it does not replace them. It openly lists what it does not know (prices, pests, water rights, salinity) and asks users to check plans with a local agronomist.

TOOLS

TypeScript, React, Vite, MapLibre GL (3D globe), Recharts, Vitest. Python for processing the GRACE / GRACE-FO mascon grid and for data-check scripts. Static site deployed on Vercel; no backend, no user data collected.

CREATIVITY

- Real NASA data turned into one practical answer: which crop, which season, which year.

- Transparent: every recommendation is traced back to data and a rule.

- "Test the future" shows whether a plan survives climate change before the farmer sows.

- Local touches: field size in sotka, a Tajik interface, satellite and map views.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Coarse data resolution (NASA POWER ~50 km, GRACE ~300 km), shown honestly in the app; slow or unavailable data services (retries, cache, and an honest "unavailable" note instead of fake numbers); weak rural internet (offline demo data); and farmers' different goals, so the tool offers several plans instead of one "right" answer.

USE OF SI

Our team came up with the idea, chose the NASA datasets, designed the three-step flow and the rotation rules, and tested the results on real fields. We used Claude (Anthropic) as an assistant for specific tasks: helping implement and debug parts of the code, drafting texts, and designing the presentation slides. All data comes from NASA and SoilGrids, not from SI, and every result was checked by our team.

Live: https://kisht-inky.vercel.app · Code: https://github.com/Alijon00/kishtWEB
